chapter: Last tours and the state of English jazz
title: Lewis Nelson in Italy, George Lewis's final tour and collapse, 1966-67
summary: Tour of Italy with Lewis Nelson, George Lewis's last tour and illness in Manchester, then Stagg's writing, later brief visits and the Olympia Brass Band in 1967.

story.theme_name: Illness, injury and the deaths of colleagues
story.community_name: Illness, injury and death among jazz musicians

blocks.x: about six or eight of them, they had about five records between them. And they had written and asked me, in fact, if they could have Chic and Handy, but they'd left it so late it was impossible to organise anything with Chic and Handy, but we said the next musician we bring to England, we would offer them. We offered them Lewis Nelson, and they jumped at the idea. So we flew with Nelson to Milan. Now Lewis Nelson was the first New Orleans musician ever to go to Italy. And it has worked out today that he's paved the way for every subsequent musician that comes to England now takes in Italy as well. So Nelson paved the way. He was a tremendous success in Italy, and they wanted him to stay longer, although being under contract with us he couldn't. We played in Milan, in Genoa, smaller places, Sandrio for the finish of an Italian professional cycle race, I remember. And we played, these cyclists all arrived, and they gave out the trophies, and we played the session afterwards. And Nelson was so popular, although none of us spoke Italian, and very few of these Italians spoke English. We sort of communicated through the music, and were treated so well, it was really something quite fantastic. They looked after us in the best hotels, and we only worked about, we were there in Italy about ten days, and we only did about five jobs in ten days, and they looked after us all the time. We went down to Genoa to do a job in a club in Genoa, the Louisiana Jazz Club in Genoa, which is in a little courtyard, rather like a New Orleans patio, rather of the soul of a court of two sisters in fact. And this little club is a fantastic club, they've got all posters, stuck all round the walls, and they've got various trophies, which they give to themselves. They've got their own little band, the Louisiana Jazz Band, who play only about once every two months. They have a session, and they've got this whole jazz club there, and no one ever comes, and they just play for themselves. And now, of course, they've got all the photographs of the Nelson tour, and probably, Nelson was the only person I went to Italy with, but they've probably got photographs of the other musicians there as well now. And this place was packed solid for about two nights, and this is the only time this has ever happened there. And we had a really fantastic time. This was, as I say, in 1966. When we came back to England, George Lewis was waiting for us. We had a second tour with George Lewis, and this was rather a sad occasion for us, really, because this was the last tour that George ever made. Before Nelson was due to return home to the States, before he went, the day before he went, we did a recording with the Barry Martin rhythm section, which was Graham Patterson on piano, Barry on drums, and Brian Turnock on bass, Cuff Billet on trumpet, George Lewis on clarinet, and Lewis Nelson on trombone. This was the only recording at that time which Nelson made in England, and turned out to be the last record George ever made. I think I'm right in saying that that's the last recording George Lewis ever made. The tour went well at the beginning. We travelled the length and breadth of this country, taken in places like Nottingham and Manchester and Birmingham. And in fact, George Lewis played one job in Birmingham with the Ken Collier band, and was the only other time between 1957 and 1966. That's the only New Orleans musician that Ken Collier had played with, between all that time. And this was the only other band that George played with on that tour. Now towards the end of the tour, that George Lewis tour, we were in the north of England. We played in Rotherham and Manchester. And we came back to London, that's the Barry Martin band. We came back to London and left George in Manchester, because of course he had his manager, manageress with him, Dorothy Tate, and she insisted on so many hours and so many days rest in between the jobs. So we decided to leave him in Manchester in the hotel. The Manchester Sports Guild, who were promoting this tour, and who had promoted the earlier tour of George Lewis with the Barry Martin band, decided and asked Dorothy Tate if George would play another job with a local band, a local Manchester-based band. As George was feeling pretty fit, and he hadn't had any illness at all while he'd been in Europe. He'd been taken to having his nasal spray and his tablets and things. And they asked Dorothy Tate if George would play one night with this local band. And if I remember correctly, Dorothy said, yes, this would be OK, providing George only played two sets of 45 minutes in the evening, with a gap in between. Well, George played the first set. This was on a Thursday night. In fact, we only had one other job to do with George. The Barry Martin band had only one other job in Nottingham to do on the Friday. Well, this was on the Thursday. We were all down in... back in London. And George played the first set with this local band and collapsed during the second set. I had a frantic telephone call. I was in bed about 7 o'clock on the Friday morning, and I had a frantic telephone call from Dorothy Tate to say George had collapsed on the stand, had been rushed into a hospital, a private room, in a hospital in Eccles, which was a suburb of Manchester. She was beside herself, really didn't know what to do. So I said, well, you stay exactly where you are, and I'll come up immediately. This is about 7 o'clock in the morning, on the Friday morning. I phoned Barry Martin and told him, well, you'd better cancel the job at Nottingham and tell them that we couldn't do this job because George had been taken as sick at that time, not knowing what was wrong with him. And I rushed up to Manchester by train to see Dorothy Tate. I met her in the hotel, and she was really in a bad way. She was beside herself, didn't know what to do, what to say or anything. I said, well, the only thing we can do is go out and see George and see how he is. At that time, she hadn't seen George. They'd taken him to hospital. So we went over to this hospital in Eccles, which is way out of Manchester, and saw George in this private room. He really did look sick. I'd only seen him about two days previously to this, and he was so full of life and had felt better than he said. He'd felt better than he had for months. And he was laid on the bed, naked on the top of the bed, and he looked so ill and drawn. He'd knock the stuffing clean out of him. One extra job would just sort of click. But of course, knowing George as we knew him, he said there was nothing wrong with him, and he'd be out of bed in about two days. He was fussing, and because Dorothy Tate was making such a fuss over him, he was getting annoyed, and seemed quite happy in his own way. And I sorted out what had to be done as far as each other's jobs were concerned, and that, of course, our contract had been broken, and that nothing would come of this, and I tied up the loose ends with the Manchester Sports Guild and came back to London. Of course, we had no work then. Our jobs... We had this one other job which had been cancelled, so I said to Barry, we will take it easy for the rest of these couple of days, and I'll go back up to Manchester at the end of the following week, which I did. George was still in hospital when I went up there. He was much better walking about in the room, and Dorothy said she'd made arrangements for him to fly home. Just before he flew home to New York, from Manchester to New York, I left and I came back to... I said cheerio in Manchester to George. In fact, that was the last time I saw George. And I heard Dorothy phone me. I phoned Dorothy just before... She made the arrangements to go back through New York before coming back home. And just before they left, Dorothy phoned me to say George had been taken sick again, but the doctor decided he could travel. And they flew him to New York, and they put him into hospital in New York, and they put him in an iron lung for... It's a couple of days, I think. And he stopped on the way down to New Orleans again, and had treatment before he ever came home. And of course, that's the last tour George ever made, and that's the last time I ever saw George was in Manchester. It was very sad. Well, that was in 19... late 1966. Uh... 1967. 1967. Uh... The... The local music scene in England had died down. It was the... the tail end of our sort of trad period. There was not too much work about... The Barry Martin band had... had... had... had personnel troubles. The trumpet player decided that his day job was far more important than the music he was playing, and decided to quit. Barry then employed Dan Pawson for a little while, from Birmingham, a band leader from Birmingham. This was not a good union at all. Barry also worked with Keith Smith. The band... didn't work much at all. I finished my business with Barry, and we went our own separate ways, although even to today we're still very friendly, and we do work a little together on the recording side, with Don taking the photographs. Uh... Nelson was called back to Italy by these Italian people, and went straight from the States to Italy, made a very long second tour, which apparently didn't go too well, whether it was because he was by himself and felt a bit out of place, I don't know. But on his way back he pulled into England, and did a couple of... I think that's right, Don, he made a couple of private jobs while he was in England. I didn't personally catch him when he came back the second time, but he made a couple of records with Barry. One with... with Mike Casimir's Brass Band, although the record came out under Barry's name, but in fact it was Mike Casimir's Brass Band, for Lacroix Records, and this was... and the second one was just Lewis Nelson with Barry Martin's band, and this is the only recording of... uh... uh... the Barry Martin Band with Dan Pawson. They only played together for a very short period. Uh... Lacroix Records were just beginning then, and this was the first, um... we heard of Lord Richard Eakins as a record producer. Before then he was just an enthusiast from Birmingham. Uh... as I say, I went my own separate way. At that time I was doing a lot of writing. I wrote a lot of sleeve notes. I did sleeve notes for George Buck. I did sleeve notes for Pearl records. The stuff for Pearl to date hasn't been used, but some of the stuff for George Buck has been used. Uh... I was writing for Jazz Journal, Jazz Times, a local book, and a small magazine from Birmingham, which I can't recall the name of at the present, and generally doing a lot of historic... historical work for New Orleans music and for the musicians in England. In fact, I have my own little archives and a record collection, which consists of, um... almost every issues recording of New Orleans music, including all the Negro bands and also the mixed bands as well, which includes the bands on tour. in... in the States, in England, and on the continent. Very few recorded examples of New Orleans musicians on the continent at present. That took us up to 1967. In 1968, Kid Sheik had a... No, late in 1967, that's right, Kid Sheik shot through England on a... very quick visit. He was in England for about one week, and I think he did two jobs as well, didn't he, Don? I thought I remember... Yeah. ... when he came back, to work mainly in Belgium and Italy. While he was there, he made a recording. Uh... in... 1967, the same applied with... John Handy. He shot through England for about one week, taking in about two jobs with the Barry Martin band, on his way to... to... going to Belgium and Italy. Uh... Halfway through 1967, of course, the Olympia Brass Band turned up, and this was the first... New Orleans Brass Band we'd ever had in England at all. Tied in with the Southern Travel Directors Council, we had really nothing at all to do with it, except we tried to organise a party. We organised a private party for the... for the fellas while they were in England, but, um... officially, we had nothing to do with the promoting of it at all. Although, fortunately, um... the... uh... UK side of the Southern Travel Directors Council allowed us to partake in all the official business which they had to do at the Hilton Hotel, and also one job for the Salvation Army. They... they allowed... they allowed us to partake in all the... what was going on, which they had to do. They included us in it, which was very nice of them, because they had no... there's no reason why they should do it, but they included us in... in these things. It was a fantastic occasion for us. We went completely mad for a couple of days, taking photographs and... and, uh... as I say, this private party, which went down very well, this... halfway through 1967. Between then and 1968, nothing happened at all. It's a completely dead period. There was the ban... the ban work was... in England has been... has been... literally nothing. The ban's really scraped around, and... and... and... mainly playing in... in sort of pub jobs, where... where... it's something like... the Kitty Halls. The ban will play in a London... or a London suburb pub, just for... for what they can get by passing...
